title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1) that evaluated whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 pairs; after preregistered exclusions 266 complete pairs were analysed. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. Paired bootstrap (B=10,000, seed=1729) 95% percentile CI = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601]. Repair was invoked for 6 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not recorded in per‑task artifacts and thus could not be evaluated. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We present preregistered design details, deterministic validator semantics, complete numeric outcomes, representative artifact‑grounded repair examples, contamination findings (no exact public duplicates flagged), and an evidence‑grounded discussion of limitations and implications.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are being actively explored for NetOps tasks such as intent→CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and maintenance workflows because they can express operator intent in natural language and produce device‑specific command sequences [1,2]. However, stochastic generation may produce syntactic or semantic violations—missing commands, unsafe ordering, or constraint breaches—that create operational risk when applied to device CLIs. To mitigate these risks, research and prototypes interpose deterministic verifiers (e.g., Batfish or related header‑space analyses) and bounded automated repair loops in generate–verify–repair (GVR) architectures so that only outputs that pass a deterministic oracle proceed toward application [3,4].

This paper reports a preregistered paired evaluation that measured the effect of allowing at most one validator‑triggered automated repair call on the same sampled initial candidate (the preregistered ‘‘shared_initial_candidate’’ estimand). Our principal scientific question (preregistered): does a GVR pipeline (single sampled initial LLM candidate + deterministic validator + ≤1 automated repair) reduce deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures compared to using the same initial candidate without repair? The study was executed under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher constraints and archived comprehensive execution and analysis artifacts. Our contribution is an artifact‑grounded, preregistered paired analysis with exact paired counts, inferential tests (exact McNemar) and a paired bootstrap interval, concrete representative before/after validator traces, and a focused threats‑to‑validity analysis that is specific to shared_initial_candidate semantics.
sections.related_work:
Prior work documents the promise and pitfalls of LLMs in NetOps. NetConfEval‑style studies and intent→CLI prototypes evaluate translation and synthesis capabilities and motivate verifier augmentation for safety [1]. Surveys of LLM applications in network operations and AIOps summarize failure modes (hallucination, syntactic mistakes, sequencing errors) that motivate grounded or tool‑augmented pipelines [2]. Generate–verify–repair architectures have been proposed across code generation and regulated domains to combine stochastic generation with deterministic oracles and bounded repair loops to converge on validator‑acceptable outputs [3]. Network verification tools such as Batfish and header‑space analyses are proposed as verifier components because they support deterministic reachability, ordering, and configuration constraint checks over a modeled topology; prototypes integrating verifiers with LLMs have been described [4]. Additionally, analyses that examine what LLMs require to synthesize correct router configurations emphasize sequencing and vendor‑syntax difficulties that verifiers can detect [5].

Our study differs by executing a preregistered paired design that (a) preserves shared_initial_candidate semantics (the same initial candidate serves as the baseline and the guarded arm’s starting point), (b) archives raw model traces and deterministic validator traces for auditability, and (c) reports exact paired contingency counts consistent with the preregistered analysis plan.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered as cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under those semantics a single sampled initial model candidate is produced per task and used to evaluate both (i) the baseline outcome (initial candidate → deterministic validator pass/fail) and (ii) the guarded outcome (same candidate → validator; if it fails, at most one automated LLM repair call is permitted and the final validator pass/fail is recorded). This paired design isolates the effect of the allowed validator‑triggered repair step for a fixed initial sample.

Task bank and sampling: The preregistered task bank deterministically produced 300 intent→CLI pairs (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like) using a deterministic synthetic task generator combined with public NetConfEval‑style examples; generation seeds and detailed per‑task manifests (including expected required sequences and allowed_touched_fields) are archived (execution/task_manifest.jsonl). Inclusion/exclusion, retry, and missingness rules followed the preregistration: both‑arm provider/infrastructure failures were excluded per the preregistered complete_pair_primary rule. Deterministic exclusion logic removed 34 both‑arm provider failures, leaving 266 complete pairs for the primary analysis (analysis/missingness_summary.csv).

Model and orchestration disclosure: The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (execution/model_configuration.json: declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Archived configuration fields include max_output_tokens = 1024, maximum_attempts_per_call = 1, provider = openai_responses, and temperature = null (unset). The orchestration adapter was hosted_netops_gvr_v1; provider call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json) records hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, and failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34. Stage accounting reports shared_initial_generation = 300 and repair = 6 (six observed repair calls). The archived null temperature does not imply a deterministically sampled output (no deterministic sampling seed was archived); thus nondeterministic provider sampling cannot be excluded.

Deterministic validator semantics: The experiment used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the binary oracle. For each candidate the validator performed: (1) syntactic parsing/normalization of CLI lines; (2) parsing into canonical commands and counting parsed_command_count; (3) comparison against per‑task required_sequence and required_command_count; (4) enforcement of allowed_fields and allowed_touched_fields; and (5) reachability/ordering checks on the seeded synthetic topology model. Episode validator traces archive validation_before and validation_after structures that include parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, normalized_configuration strings, violation codes, and a final valid flag; the valid flag is the binary pass/fail used for the primary endpoint (examples in execution/scoring/*.json).

Repair loop mechanics and constraints: Per the preregistration, the guarded arm may invoke at most one automated LLM repair call if the shared initial candidate fails the validator. Repair prompts include the validator’s failure codes, the task manifest constraints, and the normalized_failed_configuration; repair provider traces and any repair prompt SHA‑256 values are archived when invoked. The one‑repair bound was preregistered to model a constrained automated correction stage analogous to an operator’s single automated suggestion before human escalation.

Analysis plan and inferential methods: The primary confirmatory test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes (α=0.05) implemented by paired_binary_analysis_v1. For interval estimation we preregistered a paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) for the paired difference; this CI quantifies paired‑difference magnitude and finite‑sample uncertainty. We included the bootstrap CI because exact McNemar p‑values are discrete and depend only on discordant counts—reporting both aids interpretation when discordant counts are small. Missingness handling followed the preregistration (complete_pair_primary): 34 both‑arm provider failures were excluded from the primary analysis; a sensitivity analysis treated excluded pairs as failures (zero) per preregistered conservative policy.
sections.results:
Execution and failure accounting: Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2). Completed episodes = 532; failed episodes = 68 (execution_summary). Complete paired units analysed = 266; both_missing_pairs = 34 were excluded per preregistration (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider and model call accounting (deterministic_reconciliation.json): hosted_model_call_event_count = 306, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 272. Repair calls recorded = 6 (stage_counts: repair = 6). Deterministic reconciliation confirms stage accounting and that no cross‑condition cache reuse occurred.

Primary confirmatory outcomes (complete_pairs = 266): baseline successes = 260; guarded final successes = 265. Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 260 (both pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). Observed proportions: baseline = 260/266 = 0.9774436090; guarded = 265/266 = 0.9962406015. Paired difference = 0.018796992481203034. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625 (preregistered α=0.05 → not significant). Paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) = [0.0037593984962406013, 0.03759398496240601] (analysis/analysis_log.jsonl records bootstrap parameters). The bootstrap CI narrowly excludes zero while exact McNemar does not reject at α=0.05; this arises because McNemar uses only discordant counts (here 5 vs 0), producing a discrete p‑value, whereas the bootstrap CI summarizes resampled paired‑difference variability.

Repair behavior and representative artifacts: Repairs were rare (6/300). Median repair iterations per task = 0 (H2(a) confirmed). Representative task: task‑000008—shared initial candidate (execution/responses/task-000008-shared-initial.txt, sha256 = 89306095...) contained an incomplete final token "interface uplink2\n" and produced parsed_command_count mismatch; its validator trace indicated missing final command(s) and failed validation_before. The guarded final response (execution/responses/task-000008-guarded.txt, sha256 = d52b7616f...) includes the repaired full sequence that satisfied the per‑task required_sequence and passed validation_after. All such episode traces (execution/scoring/task-000008-*.json) archive the concrete violation_codes and the normalized_configuration accepted after repair, supporting reproducible inspection of repair triggers and outcomes.

Contamination and sensitivity checks: analysis/contamination_summary.csv contains no exact public‑duplicate flags; thus no tasks were excluded for contamination in the primary analysis. Sensitivity treating the 34 excluded both‑arm episodes as failures (conservative N=300) yields baseline = 260/300 = 0.866667 and guarded = 265/300 = 0.883333, with discordant counts unchanged (n10=5, n01=0) and exact McNemar p = 0.0625, indicating the primary conclusion is robust to the preregistered conservative missingness handling.

Supplementary archived artifacts: condition_summary.csv and paired_contingency_table.csv (analysis artifact hashes available) present the binary counts used for inference; deterministic_reconciliation.json documents completed_episode_count = 532 and stage_counts. The analysis executor produced analysis/results.json and archived paired_difference_figure.svg (bootstrap‑based error bars) and full logs; their SHA‑256s are recorded in analysis artifact hashes.
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation: The bounded automated repair produced a small absolute increase in validator pass‑rate (≈1.88 percentage points). Under the preregistered exact‑McNemar decision rule the improvement did not reach α=0.05 (p=0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI that excludes zero reflects resampled paired‑difference variability and can suggest practical relevance even when exact McNemar does not reject because McNemar’s p‑value is determined only by the discrete discordant counts. Reporting both perspectives clarifies this finite‑sample behavior and avoids overreliance on a single test.

Operational implications and boundary conditions: The marginal benefit of the bounded automated repair was limited because the baseline single‑shot pass rate was already high (≈97.7%), leaving few failures for repair to correct; only 6 repair invocations were recorded. These data imply that for corpora and models with high first‑pass accuracy, the operational ROI of an automated single‑repair stage may be small. Conversely, GVR might yield larger absolute gains in settings with lower first‑pass accuracy, different model sampling policies, or expanded verifier rule coverage.

Threats to validity: Internal validity—shared_initial_candidate semantics measure the effect of validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial sample and do not evaluate alternative interventions such as constrained prompting, constrained decoding, or independent multiple draws (these were not executed and are outside the estimand). Construct validity—the deterministic validator enforces a finite battery of syntactic, required‑sequence, touch‑field, and reachability checks; semantic violations outside its rule set are undetected. External validity—the task corpus is a mix of public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor dialect clusters; results may not generalize to other vendors, larger production topologies, or different difficulty distributions. Conclusion validity—few discordant pairs (n10=5, n01=0) and the loss of 34 provider‑failure pairs reduced power; future studies should plan for higher discordant counts or larger N when baseline pass rates are expected to be high.

Design lessons and reproducibility guidance: (1) Record per‑episode timing to permit evaluation of preregistered latency bounds (H2(b) could not be evaluated because per‑task latency was not archived). (2) Expand validator coverage and explicitly document validator rule sets so that construct validity and potential verifier false negatives are measurable. (3) Where investigators expect high baseline pass rates, design task banks with more difficult items or increase N to raise expected discordant counts and statistical power. (4) Reproducibility: all core execution artifacts are archived (execution/raw_results.jsonl sha256 = 34fe154d...; execution/model_configuration.json sha256 = 916b386b...), analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv sha256 = 88b65086...) and reconciliation manifests are available in the evidence bundle referenced in the preregistration; these artifacts permit exact reexecution of the paired analysis and inspection of validator traces and provider call accounting.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired experiment under shared_initial_candidate semantics, a GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) improved deterministic validator pass‑rate by 0.0188 across 266 analysed pairs but failed to meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) narrowly excludes zero. Repairs were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and could not be assessed. The study demonstrates how an artifact‑anchored preregistered paired design can quantify bounded repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics and highlights practical considerations—task difficulty selection, validator coverage, per‑episode telemetry, and expected discordant rates—necessary for future confirmatory studies aimed at operational NetOps impact.

Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Preregistration: cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). Initial master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the topic family and approved pre‑lock infrastructure development; after the autonomy lock the registered pipeline autonomously performed literature selection, preregistration, experimental execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI peer review simulation, and revision. Nondeterminism disclosure: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null (unset) and no deterministic sampling seed is archived; nondeterministic sampling of model outputs cannot be excluded for the recorded provider calls. Execution and analysis artifacts, logs, and hash manifests are archived in the evidence bundle referenced in the preregistration for audit per the track’s reproducibility requirements.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent multiple draws or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a deterministic synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
